content.text: {"relation": "REFINED", "consensus_summary": "Faith is trusting reliance on and confident assurance in God and His promises, centered on Christ for salvation; it is the instrumental means of justification and is distinguished from mere intellectual assent. Common alternatives include faith-as-faithfulness/covenant loyalty (pistis/emunah, the pistis Christou debate), 'the faith' as a body of doctrine, faith as inseparable from works, faith as divine gift, and minority views (spiritual gift, quasi-force).", "book_summary": "Faith is 'trusting faithfulness' — reliance on God's unseen promise that is held steady and brought to life (made real/complete) through obedience. The book explicitly contrasts this with the commonly taught view of faith as confident trust functioning as the sole instrument of justification.", "consensus_core_identification": "Trusting reliance on God/Christ and His promises — inward trust (fiducia), not mere assent, functioning as the instrument by which one is justified.", "book_core_identification": "Trusting faithfulness — reliance on God's unseen promise constitutively joined to and completed by obedient action.", "core_relation": "BOOK_NARROWS", "extension_relation": "BOOK_SUBSET", "boundary_disagreement": "The book makes obedience/faithfulness constitutive of faith rather than a fruit or corollary of it. Cases the mainstream consensus would count as genuine faith — inward trust that is instrumentally sufficient for justification apart from works (e.g., the classic Protestant reading of Rom 4:5 and Eph 2:8-9) — are excluded or reclassified by the book as incomplete unless 'brought to life through obedience.' The book effectively merges the consensus primary meaning with two of its listed common alternatives (faithfulness/emunah and James's faith-perfected-by-works), and its common-view note signals deliberate departure from 'sole instrument of justification' framing.", "material_contradiction": "None at the level of central referent. The book still identifies faith as reliance/trust in God's unseen promise; it does not replace trust with something else, only conditions it on obedient fidelity. The tension with 'sole instrument of justification' is a boundary/mechanics dispute (well attested within the consensus's own alternatives, e.g., James 2 and Catholic 'faith formed by love'), not a replacement of the referent.", "rationale": "Both readings identify the same referent: trust/reliance on God and His unseen promises (Heb 11:1 anchors both). The book, however, materially tightens the definition by fusing trust with faithfulness and obedience ('trusting faithfulness... brought to life through obedience'), and its common-view note explicitly flags disagreement with the standard 'sole instrument' teaching. This is real disagreement at the boundary — the book denies that bare inward trust, apart from obedient enactment, is the full biblical referent of faith — but it does not overthrow the consensus's central identification. All consensus responses list faithfulness/loyalty and faith-inseparable-from-works as common alternatives, confirming the book's move stays within a recognized category rather than being novel or contradictory. Hence REFINED, with the book narrowing the core conditions and its extension being a subset (or reclassification) of the consensus extension.", "citation_support": "STRONG", "strongest_objection": "One could argue for MATCH: several consensus responses (A's 'faith inseparable from works' alternative, C's primary meaning 'expressed through commitment, obedience... rather than mere intellectual agreement', D's 'living obedience' alternative) already fold obedience into faith, so the book merely re-weights strands the consensus itself contains. Alternatively, one could push toward DIVERGENT by reading the book's rejection of 'sole instrument of justification' as contradicting the consensus's instrumental-justification core rather than merely refining it. The REFINED verdict sits between these because the book keeps the trust-referent intact while materially changing its conditions.", "confidence": "high"}
